abstract: Ethanol, a high-demand clean energy source, is primarily produced via fed-batch fermentation in industrial settings. Although our previous study identified an optimal glucose concentration of 30 g/L for maximal ethanol yield, the mechanisms underlying glucose-dependent cellular adaptation remain unclear. Here, we performed an integrated multi-omics analysis, including transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and fluxomics, to compare yeast cells under glucose-controlled and uncontrolled conditions. Our results indicate that high glucose stress triggers the regulation of transporters with different affinities and the upregulation of heat shock proteins (HSPs), trehalose, and amino acids. In contrast, protein turnover was reduced under glucose-controlled conditions, suggesting more efficient resource allocation. This metabolic reallocation enhances carbon flux through glycolysis, potentially providing additional energy and NADH to support biomass growth and ethanol production. These findings advance our understanding of yeast regulatory mechanisms under glucose stress and provide insights for metabolic engineering and process optimization.

S

cerevisiae
was inoculated into 100 mL of activation medium in a shake flask and cultured at 30 °C with shaking at 220 rpm for 24 h. The culture was then streaked onto solid agar medium and incubated at 30 °C for 24 h. A single colony was picked and transferred into 100 mL of seed medium, followed by cultivation at 30 °C with shaking at 220 rpm. After 16 h of cultivation, when the OD
600
reached approximately 6–8, the seed culture was ready for inoculation into the fermenter.
2.2
Batch fermentation
The batch fermentation was conducted in a 5 L bioreactor with a working volume of 3 L and an inoculum size of 30 %. The fermentation temperature was maintained at 30 °C, the stirring speed was set to 150 rpm, and the pressure of bioreactors was set at 0.05 MPa to maintain stable mass transfer. The pH naturally decreased from 5.5 at the start to approximately 4.6 at the end of fermentation without external adjustment. Nitrogen gas was continuously supplied throughout the process to ensure anaerobic batch fermentation of the yeast. The batch fermentation with 285 g/L initial glucose concentration served as the control to evaluate the impact of different glucose concentration control strategies on fermentation performance.
2.3
Fed-batch fermentation
The process control conditions of fed-batch fermentation are consistent with those of batch fermentation. The fed-batch fermentation process started with an initial glucose concentration of 100 g/L. During fed-batch fermentation, when the glucose concentration decreased to 30 g/L, an intelligent feedback feeding platform was activated to dynamically maintain glucose levels at this setpoint. The total amount of glucose supplied throughout the fed-batch process was equivalent to that used in the batch fermentation. Automated feeding was triggered by a Raman spectroscopy-based predictive model, as described in our previous work [
23
]. Fermentation was terminated when the glucose concentration in the bioreactor dropped below 1 g/L.
2.4
Determination of glucose, glycerol, ethanol concentration and cell dry weight
The concentrations of glucose, glycerol, and ethanol were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) using 5 mM sulfuric acid as the mobile phase at a detection wavelength of 215 nm. The analysis was performed on an Aminex HPX-87H column with a flow rate of 0.6 mL/min and column temperature maintained at 50 °C. A 15 μL sample volume was injected for each analysis, with a total run time of 30 min per sample.
A 0.08 μm fiber filter membrane was dried in a microwave oven for 3 min and weighed. A 2 mL fermentation broth was filtered through the membrane, and washed three times with deionized water. The membrane was then dried again for 3 min and reweighed. Dry cell weight was calculated as the difference between the final and initial membrane weights.
2.5
Rapid sampling and quantification of intracellular metabolites
Approximately 1 mL of culture broth was rapidly sampled from the bioreactor using our rapid sampling device and quenched in 8 mL of −20 °C pre-cooled methanol solution (40 % v/v), with the exact weight recorded. The cells were immediately collected on the filter using a vacuum filtration system. The filter containing cells was then transferred into 40 mL of 75 % ethanol solution, followed by addition of pre-prepared U–
13
C labeled
Pichia pastoris
intracellular extracts as internal standards. Isotope dilution mass spectrometry (IDMS) method was employed to correct analytical bias and ensure accurate quantification [
30
]. Cell lysis was achieved by incubating the sample in 75 % methanol solution at 95 °C water bath for 3 min, after which the sample was stored at −80 °C for subsequent analysis. Throughout the process, rapid sampling and quenching were strictly followed to minimize alterations in intracellular metabolites.
The derivatization procedures for intracellular metabolites (including amino acids and sugar phosphates) and GC-MS analytical conditions followed the well-established methods in our laboratory as previously described [
31
,
32
].
2.6
Transcriptome analysis
Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent following the manufacturer's protocol. RNA purity and concentration were measured using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer, while RNA integrity was assessed with an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. The transcriptome library was prepared using the VAHTS Universal V5 RNA-seq Library Prep Kit according to the manufacturer's instructions. Due to its superior throughput and data quality, the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform was selected for transcriptome sequencing, with read quality control performed using fastp software. The sequencing process was performed by Shanghai OE Biotech Co., Ltd (
www.oebiotech.com
).
Differential gene expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 software using raw count data, with genes meeting the thresholds of q-value (adjusted p-value) < 0.05 and fold change >2 or < 0.5 defined as differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Principal component analysis (PCA) and correlation analysis were conducted to reveal variations and similarities among samples. Functional enrichment analysis of DEGs was carried out through KEGG pathway analyses to identify the most significantly enriched functional terms.
2.7
Proteome analysis
This study utilized TMT (Tandem Mass Tag) technology for proteomic analysis, a widely adopted approach for differential protein expression profiling. Proteins were first extracted and subjected to quality control via SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE), with only high-quality SDS-PAGE samples proceeding to subsequent processing. Following tryptic digestion, the peptides were labeled using TMT reagents. The raw mass spectrometry data were processed through database searching for both identification and quantification, followed by differential expression analysis and functional characterization. The proteome detection process was performed by Shanghai OE Biotech Co., Ltd (
www.oebiotech.com
).
To identify a sufficient number of differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), we directly considered proteins with q-value <0.05 as statistically significant. PCA and correlation analysis were performed to reveal inter-sample variations and similarities. Functional enrichment analysis of DEPs was conducted through KEGG pathway analyses to identify the most significantly enriched functional terms.
2.8
Metabolic flux distribution simulation
Constraint-based modeling was implemented in this study using the published
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
model Yeast8 [
33
]. Flux distributions were generated through sampling methods, with experimentally measured exchange rates of glucose, ethanol and glycerol serving as the constraints, and oxygen uptake was zero to simulate the anaerobic environment. The solution space was randomly sampled to obtain 10,000 points, yielding flux distributions for each reaction. Relative flux values were calculated as each reaction flux percentage relative to the glucose uptake rate.

1
Introduction
Ethanol is widely used in energy production, industrial solvents, and food applications [
1
,
2
]. With the depletion of global petrochemical resources and increasing environmental awareness, fuel ethanol has gained growing recognition as an alternative to conventional energy sources such as petroleum, coal and natural gas [
[3]
,
[4]
,
[5]
]. The use of fuel ethanol contributes to optimizing energy infrastructure, reducing petroleum dependence, lowering carbon emissions, and protecting ecological systems [
6
,
7
]. However, biological manufacturing still operates in a relatively extensive manner, largely due to inadequate implementation of process monitoring and regulation [
8
,
9
].
Currently, ethanol production can be categorized into batch fermentation, fed-batch fermentation, continuous fermentation, and semi-continuous fermentation [
[10]
,
[11]
,
[12]
]. Due to technical and cost issues in industrial production, batch fermentation is typically conducted under high sugar concentration conditions [
13
]. Although this fermentation process is simple to operate, it also increases the osmotic pressure and substrate inhibition in the cell culture environment and boosts the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and glycerol [
14
,
15
], which negatively impacts ethanol fermentation. To avoid the inhibitory effects of high sugar concentrations, some industrial ethanol fermentations have adopted simultaneous saccharification and fermentation processes [
16
]. Nevertheless, significant fluctuations in glucose concentration may still occur during the saccharification process. In this context, compared to traditional batch fermentation methods for ethanol production, fed-batch fermentation technology effectively avoids the inhibitory effects of high sugar concentrations on the fermentation process by maintaining the sugar concentration at a lower and more stable level, thereby reducing the production of by-products [
17
].
To our knowledge, a few studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of feeding strategies in improving ethanol production. For example, Feng et al. implemented a dual-feeding approach to maintain glucose concentration below 100 g/L during fermentation, resulting in a 15.4 % increase in ethanol yield and 9.04 % improvement in sugar-to-ethanol conversion rate compared to batch fermentation [
18
]. Similarly, Chang et al. achieved a total sugar concentration of 260 g/L by supplementing sugar under an initial glucose concentration of 180 g/L, resulting in an ethanol production of 130.1 g/L. This represents a 12 % increase in ethanol yield compared to batch fermentation with the same total sugar concentration [
19
]. However, these feeding approaches remain empirical and imprecise. To enable more accurate fermentation monitoring, online sensor technologies such as machine learning-based Raman spectroscopy models for predicting metabolite concentration are being implemented [
[20]
,
[21]
,
[22]
]. Furthermore, our prior research on controlled fed-batch fermentation demonstrated that maintaining lower glucose concentrations during the fermentation process favors ethanol production [
23
]. Despite advances in feeding strategies that enhance ethanol production, the mechanisms by which cell regulate their metabolism under optimal glucose concentrations remains poorly understood.
The advent of multi-omics technologies has greatly deepened our understanding of microbial physiology in industrial biotechnology. In ethanol fermentation, different omics layers have uncovered distinct cellular responses to environmental stresses such as high sugar concentrations and ethanol toxicity. These responses include changes in gene expression [
24
,
25
], modulation of key enzymes and stress-related proteins [
26
,
27
], and alterations in metabolite levels and metabolic flux distributions [
28
,
29
]. However, most existing studies rely on single or dual omics approaches, providing only a partial view of the complex regulatory landscape. A systematic integration of transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and fluxomic data is therefore urgently needed to comprehensively elucidate the molecular networks underlying yeast metabolic regulation under different fermentation strategies.
In this study, we conducted a comparative omics analysis to investigate the cell regulatory mechanism under two contrasting glucose conditions: uncontrolled glucose levels in batch and optimally controlled glucose levels in fed-batch fermentation, the latter achieved via a Raman spectroscopy-based feedback control strategy. By integrating transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and fluxomic analyses, this study aimed to elucidate the biological impact of glucose concentration on yeast physiology and ethanol production, providing new insights into metabolic regulation for more efficient bioethanol manufacturing.

3
Results
3.1
Glucose concentration dictates ethanol production performance by
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Batch fermentation in a 5 L bioreactor, with an initial glucose concentration of 285 g/L, yielded 125.71 g/L of ethanol and 10.23 g/L of glycerol after 48 h (
Fig. 1
A). To improve ethanol yield, we previously established an intelligent feedback feeding platform. It enables accurate prediction and control of residual glucose levels using an online Raman spectrometer in combination with a PID algorithm [
23
], and it is adaptable to various feeding scenarios (
Fig. S1
). By comparing different feeding strategies, it was found that initiating fermentation with 100 g/L glucose followed by controlled glucose supplementation significantly enhanced ethanol production, particularly when the glucose concentration was maintained at 30 g/L, resulting in the highest ethanol yield and reduced fermentation time (
Fig. S1
). When scaled up to a 50 L bioreactor, this glucose-controlled strategy similarly enhanced ethanol production efficiency (
Fig. S2
). Therefore, subsequent experiments focused on investigating the metabolic differences between the fed-batch fermentation maintaining glucose concentration at 30 g/L (hereafter referred to as process FB30) and batch fermentation (hereafter referred to as process B285) (
Fig. 1
A).
Fig. 1
Physiological profiles of batch fermentation and fed-batch fermentation of
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
in 5 L bioreactor.
(A) The fed-batch fermentation was performed with an initial glucose concentration of 100 g/L and glucose concentration controlled at 30 g/L thereafter. Data in the plots are shown with mean ± s.d. of three biological replicates. (B) Physiological parameters of different fermentation conditions.
Fig. 1
Comparative analysis between FB30 and B285 demonstrated that under the same total glucose mass, the glucose-controlled feeding strategy significantly enhanced fermentation performance relative to batch fermentation. The cell dry weight increased by 1.27-fold from 10.32 g/L to 13.12 g/L by the end of fermentation. Ethanol concentration improved from 125.71 g/L to 140.68 g/L, while glycerol byproduct decreased from 10.23 g/L to 6.72 g/L. Notably, the fermentation duration was reduced from 48 h to 39 h (
Fig. 1
B). Furthermore, FB30 exhibited significantly higher specific growth rates and specific ethanol production rates along with lower specific glycerol production rates compared to B285. Meanwhile, the productivity was increased from 3.39 g/L/h to 5.34 g/L/h. Since the glucose concentration throughout the batch fermentation process was always higher than that of the fed-batch fermentation, these metabolic alterations conclusively indicate that controlled glucose concentration significantly impacted yeast cell physiology and effectively redirected cellular metabolic fluxes.
3.2
Identification of differentially expressed genes and proteins between glucose-controlled fed-batch and uncontrolled batch fermentation
To elucidate the cellular adaptation mechanism of
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
cells under glucose-controlled fermentation, we performed a comparative omics (transcriptome, proteome, metabolome and fluxome) analysis of two different fermentation processes. Samples were collected at the exponential phase (7 h) and stationary phase (25 h) for both fermentation processes, with three biological replicates per group. In the glucose-controlled fermentation process, samples taken at 7 h and 25 h were designated as FB30-7h and FB30-25h, respectively. For the batch fermentation process, the corresponding samples were labeled as B285-7h and B285-25h.
Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on transcriptomic and proteomic data separately (
Fig. S3
). The results showed high dispersion between different time points, indicating significant differences across distinct phases. Within-group samples exhibited tight clustering, demonstrating high similarity and good reproducibility. Meanwhile, Pearson correlation coefficients revealed that intra-group sample correlations were nicely close to 1 for both transcriptomic and proteomic data, confirming high experimental reproducibility (
Fig. S3
). Notably, inter-group correlations were higher in proteomic data than in transcriptomic data, which may be that gene expression is easily influenced by environmental changes [
34
] and mRNAs are less stable than proteins [
35
].
Furthermore, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with the thresholds of |log2FC|>1 and q-value<0.05. Compared with B285, FB30 exhibited 214 significantly upregulated genes and 222 downregulated genes at 7 h, while showing 415 upregulated genes and 558 downregulated genes at 25 h (
Fig. 2
). However, to identify a sufficient number of differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), we directly considered proteins with q-value <0.05 as statistically significant. Compared with B285, FB30 demonstrated 45 significantly upregulated proteins and 115 downregulated proteins at 7 h, while showing 13 upregulated proteins and 8 downregulated proteins at 25 h (
Fig. 2
).
Fig. 2
Differential analysis of transcriptome and proteome.
The left panel shows the volcano plot of the differential genes or proteins of FB30 versus B285, and the right panel shows the pathways of Top20 of the corresponding KEGG enrichment analysis. Symbol ∗ represents a significantly enriched pathway for q-value <0.05.
Fig. 2
Subsequently, to further investigate the biological functions of these differentially expressed genes and proteins, we performed KEGG enrichment analysis (
Fig. 2
). At 7 h, the DEGs primarily showed downregulation of ribosome pathways, which correlated with cellular growth under different fermentation conditions. The DEPs mainly exhibited downregulation of proteasome, consistent with the ribosome downregulation trend observed in transcriptome data, which was correlated with FB30 cells entering the late exponential growth phase substantially earlier than B285 cells during this cultivation period. Moreover, the absence of the high-sugar environment meant that the FB30 condition did not require the synthesis of stress-response proteins, thus eliminating the associated protein turnover. At 25 h, the DEGs were predominantly characterized by downregulation of glycolysis/gluconeogenesis and various carbon metabolism pathways, associated with lower glucose uptake under low sugar concentration conditions (
Fig. 1
B). There were few DEPs and no significant enrichment in any pathway, indicating that glucose concentration no longer affected cell metabolism pathway, as we measured the comparable glucose levels at this time. Related studies confirmed high glucose concentration stress can cause significant changes in genes involved in protein modification, RNA metabolism, stress response, and transcription in
S. cerevisiae
ethanol fermentation [
36
], which was also reflected in our study.
Furthermore, comparative transcriptomic and proteomic analyses were performed at different time points within each fermentation mode (
Fig. S4
). Under the B285 condition, when comparing 25 h–7 h, numerous significantly downregulated genes were enriched in the ribosome pathway, while downregulated proteins were predominantly associated with the proteasome pathway. These results suggest that cells reduced energy-intensive processes such as protein synthesis and degradation. This trend is consistent with the enrichment patterns observed in the FB30-7h vs. B285-7h comparison, indicating that glucose concentration influenced the expression of these genes and proteins. A lower glucose concentration appeared to decrease protein turnover [
37
], thereby promoting a more efficient resource allocation strategy to support enhanced biomass and ethanol production. In contrast, in the FB30-25h vs. FB30-7h comparison, differentially expressed genes were also enriched in the ribosome pathway, though to a lesser extent than in the B285 condition, suggesting a milder effect of glucose limitation on ribosomal activity. Moreover, no significant pathway enrichment was observed among differentially abundant proteins, implying that the fed-batch process maintained a more stable metabolic state.
3.3
Proteome reallocation explains ethanol production improvement under glucose-controlled condition
In the central carbon metabolic pathways, FB30 exhibited significant downregulation (q-value<0.05) of most glycolytic genes compared to B285 at 7 h or 25 h (
Fig. 3
A), indicating high glucose concentrations induce glycolytic gene expression to metabolize the abundant environmental glucose. In the proteomic data, phosphofructokinase isoforms (PFK1 and PFK2) were the only glycolytic enzymes significantly downregulated at 7 h in the fed-batch fermentation. This likely reflects the substantial difference in glucose availability between the two fermentation modes at this stage. Under batch fermentation, higher levels of this key rate-limiting enzyme are required to process abundant extracellular glucose and mitigate associated stress. For the TCA cycle and pentose phosphate pathway, most genes and proteins showed minimal (|log2FC|<1) or insignificant (q-value>0.05) changes, demonstrating that different glucose feeding strategies had limited impact on these pathways. This observation aligns with the fact that ethanol production predominantly occurs via glycolysis pathway under anaerobic conditions [
29
].
Fig. 3
Analysis of transcriptomics and proteomics data.
(A) Heat map of the differential expression genes (DEGs). White background indicates the genes or proteins with no significant differences. The transcriptomic samples were obtained from three biological replicates. (B) Comparison of abundance of partial differential expression proteins (DEPs) between different fermentation conditions. The proteomic samples were obtained from three biological replicates.
Fig. 3
We subsequently analyzed genes and proteins involved in ethanol production. Pyruvate serves as a crucial precursor for ethanol synthesis, which can be converted to acetaldehyde by pyruvate decarboxylase (PDC) under anaerobic conditions. Among the three PDC isoforms, PDC1 plays the dominant role and represents a key regulatory point for enhancing pyruvate flux toward ethanol [
38
]. In our experiments, PDC genes and proteins showed significant downregulation in FB30-7h (
Fig. 3
A and B), and PDC1 mRNA expression in FB30-25h increased 1.94-fold compared to B285-25h (
Fig. 3
A), while its protein level remained stable, indicating that yeast cells regulate acetaldehyde production flux not through enzyme expression levels, but rather via other regulatory factors, as evidenced by studies showing inhibition of PDC activity under high glucose concentrations [
39
]. Acetaldehyde is subsequently reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH). Among the six ADH isoforms, ADH2, ADH4 and ADH6 showed upregulated gene expression in FB30 (
Fig. 3
A), consistent with previous studies [
40
,
41
]. High glucose concentration inhibits ADH2 transcription through the transcriptional activator Adr1p. However, ADH4 and ADH6 primarily metabolize other alcohols [
42
,
43
] and shows minimal involvement in acetaldehyde-ethanol conversion. Therefore, we propose ADH4 and ADH6 as potential engineering knockout target for developing high-ethanol-producing strains.
Furthermore, aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALD), which converts acetaldehyde into the byproduct acetate, showed significantly downregulated protein expression in FB30 at 7 h (
Fig. 3
B). Related studies have proved that fed-batch fermentation can reduce the production of acetate compared with batch fermentation [
44
]. Studies have also shown that knocking out the ALD6 gene of
S. cerevisiae
reduced acetate production [
45
,
46
], so it could also be used as a target for this strain to reduce ethanol production. Additionally, we observed reduced glycerol production in the FB30 fermentation phenotype. To investigate this, we analyzed the glycerol biosynthesis pathway, glycerol is primarily synthesized through the catalysis of glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) to produce glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P), which is subsequently dephosphorylated by glycerol-3-phosphatase (GPP). In
S. cerevisiae
, GPD1 and GPD2 represent two isoforms of the rate-limiting enzyme GAPDH in glycerol synthesis, with GPD1 playing the predominant regulatory role [
47
]. In this study, under glucose-controlled conditions, both gene expression levels of GPD1, GPP1, and GPP2 were significantly downregulated at both 7 h and 25 h (
Fig. 3
A), which are consistent with previous research by Deng et al. [
44
]. These results demonstrated that the glucose-controlled strategy effectively reduces byproducts formation, thereby directing more carbon flux toward ethanol production.
Compared with B285, FB30 showed significantly upregulated mRNA levels of both HXT6 and HXT7 at 7 h and 25 h (
Fig. 3
A). HXT6 and HXT7 belong to the glucose transporter (HXT) gene family, and previous studies have demonstrated that these genes are highly expressed under low extracellular glucose concentrations but suppressed under high glucose conditions [
48
,
49
]. As high-affinity glucose transporters, their upregulated expression enables cells to maximize glucose uptake under glucose-controlled conditions, thereby ensuring that the glucose uptake rate does not drop significantly compared to that under glucose-uncontrolled conditions (
Fig. 1
B). Conversely, under high glucose concentrations, cells typically suppress these high-affinity transporters while upregulating low-affinity transporters like HXT1 and HXT3 [
50
]. Furthermore, A-agglutinin-binding subunit (AGA2) in
S. cerevisiae
participates in cell surface ligand binding, and its expression enhances the interaction between transporters and glucose, thereby improving glucose uptake [
51
]. We observed significant upregulation of AGA2 protein levels, with 3.87-fold and 1.73-fold increases at 7 h and 25 h, respectively. These findings suggested that under glucose-controlled conditions,
S. cerevisiae
not only expresses high-affinity glucose transporters but also upregulates ligand-binding proteins to enhance glucose uptake.
As displayed in
Fig. 3
A, different glucose supply strategies also induced expression variations in stress-responsive genes such as the PAU family. The PAU genes represent the largest gene family in
S. cerevisiae
, becoming active during ethanol fermentation and being negatively regulated by oxygen availability. They are associated with yeast's response to various stresses including hypoxia, high glucose, high ethanol, low pH, and thermal fluctuations [
52
,
53
]. At 7 h, most PAU genes in FB30 showed significant upregulation. This indicated that the upregulation of PAU genes in this study was not due to hypoxia and high glucose concentration, but probably due to higher ethanol concentrations under glucose-controlled condition. Additionally, heat-shock proteins (HSPs) responding to thermal/osmotic stress and trehalose synthesis-related trehalose 6-phosphate synthase (Tps) proteins were predominantly downregulated in FB30. This pattern indicated their elevated expression under high glucose concentration conditions helps counteract the glucose stress.
3.4
Upregulation of intracellular metabolites in response to glucose concentration stress
To further investigate the metabolic differences between the two strategies, we measured intracellular concentrations of metabolites including amino acids, sugar phosphates, organic acids, and sugar alcohols (
Fig. 4
). Significant differences were observed in four amino acids at 7 h (alanine, leucine, serine, and ornithine) and six amino acids at 25 h (alanine, glycine, proline, serine, threonine, and ornithine). Most amino acids showed lower concentrations in FB30 compared to B285. On the one hand, the cells increased protein expression to adapt to stress such as high sugar stress under B285 conditions. On the other hand, cells allocated more resources for growth and ethanol generation under FB30 conditions. Alanine, serving as a key metabolic intermediate in various biosynthesis and catabolism pathways, can be converted to pyruvate via alanine aminotransferase (encoded by ALT2). Proteomic data revealed ALT2 was upregulated 1.1-fold and 1.08-fold in FB30 at 7 h and 25 h, respectively. Consistent with this, we observed that the alanine concentration of batch fermentation was higher than that of fed-batch fermentation. Similar concentration patterns were observed for glycine, valine, leucine and serine, all of which are also capable of interconvert with pyruvate. Their reduced levels in FB30 indicate enhanced carbon flux toward pyruvate-derived products rather than amino acid biosynthesis. Simultaneously, we observed higher ornithine concentrations in FB30 compared to B285. This accumulation could facilitate the biosynthesis of arginine and glutamate, which can protect both cell wall and cytoplasm membrane against high ethanol stress [
28
,
54
].

3.5
Energy metabolism drives the altered ethanol production flux
Flux allows us to analyze metabolic differences under different conditions more intuitively. To this end, we compared the relative flux distribution results obtained from sampling methods [
62
,
63
] for FB30 and B285 at 7 h (
Fig. 5
A). In the central carbon metabolic pathway, FB30 allocated more carbon through the glycolysis pathway, generating relatively more NADH. To maintain redox balance within the cells, the ethanol production reaction provided a means for NADH disposal, thus accompanying an increase in ethanol production (
Fig. 1
) and CO
2
production (
Fig. S5
). Meanwhile, this flux pattern also generated more ATP, which was used for cell growth, as evidenced by the observation that FB30 exhibited higher biomass in the experiments. As shown by the transcriptome and proteome results, higher biomass and ethanol yields were achieved with reduced protein turnover. Conversely, B285 allocated more carbon towards the production of byproducts such as glycerol. Under high glucose concentration conditions, cells allocated more resources to cope with high glucose concentration stress, such as stress-resistant proteins, amino acids, and trehalose as part of their stress response mechanisms. Moreover, there were no significant differences in the flux distribution of the TCA cycle and the pentose phosphate pathway, indicating that different feeding strategies have little impact on these pathways, which was consistent with results obtained from transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics (
Fig. 3
,
Fig. 4
). Similarly, the flux distribution at 25 h reflected the same conclusions as at 7 h (
Fig. S6
), indicating that maintaining low glucose concentration increases final ethanol yield while reducing byproduct formation. Using sampled flux distributions, we calculated ATP production efficiency under both conditions, revealing significantly higher ATP production rates per unit glucose uptake flux in glucose-controlled fermentation (
Fig. 5
B). Furthermore, under this condition, the cells do not need to allocate more ATP to cope with energy-consuming responses to stress, such as amino acid metabolism [
[64]
,
[65]
,
[66]
], and this results in more energy available for cell growth.

4
Discussion
This study systematically compared the metabolic differences of
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
between fed-batch fermentation with precise glucose concentration control and batch fermentation. Compared to batch fermentation, maintaining 30 g/L glucose concentration increased ethanol yield by 11.9 %, reduced fermentation time by 9 h, and decreased glycerol byproduct concentration by 34.3 %. In this study, we elucidated the cellular regulatory mechanisms that glucose-controlled fermentation improved ethanol production through integrated multi-omics and metabolic flux analysis approaches (
Fig. 6
). At 30 g/L glucose, yeast cells under non-stress conditions enhanced glycolytic flux to generate additional ATP and NADH, providing energy for biomass growth and increasing ethanol production to maintain redox balance. Although we have a reasonable explanation for the flux-based results, further verification is needed. Meanwhile, compared with a large range of changes in glucose concentration in batch fermentation, glucose-controlled condition provided a stable glucose concentration environment, allowing for consistently high ethanol production. In contrast, batch fermentation with high glucose concentrations triggered transporter adaptations and upregulation of stress-responsive proteins and metabolites to counteract stress. Under such condition, more glycerol was produced, which was also considered as a stress-resistant metabolite that cannot be replaced by sugar alcohols [
58
,
67
]. Taken together, it is most likely the production of these stress-resistant metabolites that causes the cells to allocate less carbon through the glycolysis pathway, consequently reducing ethanol biosynthesis. Furthermore, the integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed pronounced alterations in ribosome-related genes and proteasome-associated proteins across different fermentation modes and time points. These results indicate that fed-batch fermentation reduces protein turnover, enabling cells to achieve higher biomass and ethanol yields through more efficient protein allocation—an observation not previously reported. In contrast to earlier studies on sugar concentration that employed batch fermentation or empirical feeding strategies [
19
,
[68]
,
[69]
,
[70]
], our work was performed under precisely controlled glucose levels, thereby minimizing metabolic fluctuations arising from substrate variability.

Although glucose levels were precisely regulated using intelligent feedback feeding, which significantly enhanced ethanol production, alternative feeding strategies such as linear or exponential adapted feeding [
10
], may achieve even higher yields. The effectiveness of these approaches under more precise glucose control warrants further investigation. In addition, the identification of an optimal initial glucose concentration for fed-batch fermentation [
71
] remains a topic for future research. Ethanol production is influenced by multiple factors, and the substantial formation of byproducts such as glycerol and acetate highlights considerable potential for yield improvement. Such optimization could be achieved through fermentation process refinement or targeted metabolic engineering to reduce glycerol synthesis or enable its metabolic utilization [
72
,
73
]. While this study proposes that knocking out genes such as ADH4, ADH6, and ALD6 may enhance ethanol production, experimental validation is still required. Furthermore, ethanol itself imposes a critical limitation due to cellular toxicity at high concentrations. Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) of engineered strains represents a promising strategy to simultaneously improve ethanol production and ethanol tolerance [
74
,
75
]. The integration of high-performance strains with optimized fermentation processes will be essential for advancing industrial ethanol production.
The substantial differences in gene expression observed between fermentation modes in this study provide valuable insights for metabolic engineering. However, the corresponding variations at the protein and metabolite levels were less pronounced. Several factors may contribute to this discrepancy. First, proteins are generally more stable than mRNA, and excessive protein turnover can impose additional metabolic burdens on the cell [
76
]. Moreover, discrepancies between transcriptomic and proteomic changes may result from multiple layers of regulation, including transcriptional control, RNA degradation, post-translational modification, and protein stability [
56
,
77
,
78
]. At the metabolite level, post-translational regulation likely explains the weak correlation between metabolite abundance and protein expression [
79
]. Key glycolytic enzymes, such as phosphofructokinase, are subject to complex allosteric regulation and phosphorylation, enabling rapid metabolic adjustments that occur before slower proteomic remodeling. Furthermore, metabolite concentrations represent the integrated outcomes of all enzymatic reactions within the network, rather than simple reflections of enzyme abundance. Factors such as substrate availability, enzyme saturation, feedback inhibition, and thermodynamic constraints collectively shape the final metabolic profile [
55
,
57
,
80
,
81
]. Overall, these multilayered regulatory processes highlight the complexity of linking transcriptional, proteomic, and metabolic responses, and point to promising directions for future research aimed at elucidating dynamic cellular adaptation mechanisms.
5
Conclusions
In this study, we demonstrated that glucose-controlled fed-batch fermentation, enabled by intelligent feedback feeding technology, significantly enhanced ethanol production compared with glucose-uncontrolled batch fermentation. Regulation of glucose levels reshaped the cellular proteome, promoting a resource allocation strategy that favored biomass accumulation and ethanol synthesis. In contrast, batch fermentation under high-glucose stress induced the upregulation of stress-response genes and the accumulation of intracellular sugar alcohols. Moreover, flux analysis suggested that glucose-controlled conditions altered cellular energy metabolism, thereby supporting higher ethanol yields.
